summary: Chinese numbers are perfectly regular: learn 零 and 一 to 十, then 百 and 千, and every number is built like a sum — 十一 ‘ten-one’ = 11, 二十 ‘two-ten’ = 20, 二十一 = 21, 九十九 = 99. A number never stands right before a noun: number + measure word + noun (三本书 ‘three books’, 两个人 ‘two people’), and for ‘two’ before a measure word you say 两, not 二. The noun itself never changes, so quantity words do the work of a plural: 很多 ‘many’, 一些 ‘some’, 都 ‘all’.

blocks.title: Age needs no verb
blocks.text: 我二十岁 ‘I am twenty’, 这个孩子两岁 ‘this child is two’ — number + 岁, no 是 and no 有.

blocks.title: Tens before units
blocks.text: Chinese says a number in the order of its digits, tens before units: 二十一 ‘two-ten-one’ = 21. German says the units first (einundzwanzig ‘one-and-twenty’); Chinese never does.

blocks.title: Never number + noun
blocks.text: *三书, *两人 are wrong: 三本书, 两个人. The measure word is as obligatory as the German article.

blocks.title: No plural after a number
blocks.text: The noun never takes a plural — not after a number and not anywhere else: 两本书, 十个人, 很多书.

askYourself: Is there a noun after the number? → put its measure word in between: 三本书, 两个人.
Is it ‘two’ right before a measure word? → 两 (两个, 两岁). Counting, inside numbers, ordinals, digits → 二 (十二, 二十, 第二).
Is it 11–19? → 十 + digit (十五). A round ten? → digit + 十 (五十). In between? → digit + 十 + digit (五十五).
Is a place empty inside a bigger number (101, 1005)? → say 零 once: 一百零一, 一千零五.
Is it an age? → number + 岁, with no 是: 他十八岁.
How is 一 said here? Alone, counting, at the end → yī; before a 4th tone → yí; before tones 1–3 → yì.
Do I mean ‘many / few’? → 很多 before the noun; 多, 少, 不多, 很少 after it as the predicate (人很多, 人很少).
Do I mean ‘all’? → 都 right before the verb, often with 所有 / 这些 / 我们 before it.
steps: Say the number in written order (二十一 = 2-10-1).

traps: *两十 → 二十; and inside numbers it is always 二: 十二个, 二十二个 (not *十两个).
10 is 十, never *一十 — but 110 is 一百一十.
*三书 → 三本书: the measure word cannot be left out.
*少人 / *多人 → 人很少 / 很多人: 多 and 少 alone do not stand before a noun.
*他是十八岁 in a plain statement → 他十八岁.
*都我们是学生 → 我们都是学生: 都 stands before the verb.

quiz.why: Before a measure word ‘two’ is 两, and the measure word 本 is needed.
Inside numbers 2 is always 二; 二十 is 20.
零 fills the empty tens; 一百一 would be heard as 110.
Age: number + 岁, no verb and no 个.

quiz.q: How is 一 said in 一个?
quiz.why: Before a 4th tone (个 was gè) 一 becomes yí.

quiz.q: ‘There are a lot of people here.’
quiz.why: The amount comes last as the predicate: 人很多.
都 stands right before the verb.

notes.text: Greek numbers are also tens first (είκοσι ένα ~ 二十一), but 1, 3 and 4 agree in gender (ένας / μία / ένα, τρεις / τρία) and the noun is plural. Chinese numbers never change, the noun never changes, and a measure word goes in between.
Russian один / одна and два / две agree, and the noun changes its case after numbers (два стола, пять столов). Chinese has nothing to agree: 两张桌子, 五张桌子 — only the measure word.
Spanish veintiuno is tens first, like 二十一, and uno / una agree with the noun while 一 never changes. Spanish has one word for two; Chinese has 二 for counting and 两 before a measure word.
English twenty-one has the order of 二十一, but eleven to nineteen are irregular; in Chinese even 11–19 are regular: 十一 ‘ten-one’. And the noun takes no -s: 三本书.
French counts partly in twenties (soixante-dix ‘sixty-ten’ = 70, quatre-vingts ‘four-twenties’ = 80); Chinese is purely decimal: 七十 ‘seven-ten’, 八十 ‘eight-ten’.
German einundzwanzig puts the units first; Chinese 二十一 follows the written order. Where German counts directly (drei Bücher), Chinese adds a measure word: 三本书.

Hindi numbers from 11 to 99 are each a separate word, units first (इक्कीस 21, बयालीस 42); Chinese builds every number from ten digits, tens first: 二十一, 四十二. Large numbers: Hindi groups by lakh and crore, Chinese by ten thousand (万, later).

Persian numbers are tens first, joined by o (bist-o-yek ‘twenty-and-one’); Chinese simply strings them: 二十一. Persian also keeps the noun singular after a number (se ketāb) and may add tā — Chinese must add a measure word.
Marathi has a separate, irregular word for each number up to 100, units first (एकवीस 21); Chinese builds all of them regularly, tens first: 二十一.

Arabic says units before tens (wāḥid wa-ʿishrūn ‘one and twenty’), and the numerals 3–10 take the opposite gender of the noun; Chinese says tens first (二十一) and never agrees. Arabic has a dual (kitābān ‘two books’); Chinese says 两本书.
Hebrew numbers agree in gender with the noun, which is plural; Chinese numbers never change and the noun stays bare: 三本书.
Turkish also keeps the noun singular after numbers (iki kitap) and says tens first (yirmi bir ~ 二十一); Chinese goes further — the noun never has a plural — and adds a measure word: 两本书.
Sino-Japanese numbers are built exactly like Chinese ones (二十一 nijūichi), and Japanese also needs counters. 万 man ‘ten thousand’ will be Chinese 万 wàn too.

Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼 …, 이십일 ‘21’) follow the Chinese pattern exactly, and Korean also needs counters. Korean’s second, native set (하나, 둘, 셋) has no Chinese counterpart; the Chinese split is 二 / 两.
Finnish kaksikymmentäyksi ‘two-ten-one’ has the Chinese order; but Finnish puts the noun in the partitive after numbers (kolme kirjaa), while Chinese adds a measure word (三本书).
Hungarian has two forms of ‘two’ — kettő alone, két before a noun — much like Chinese 二 / 两 (两 before a measure word). Hungarian also keeps the noun singular after numbers (két könyv ~ 两本书).

Swahili numerals follow the noun, and some agree with its class (vitabu viwili ‘two books’); Chinese numerals come first and never change: 两本书. Swahili ishirini na moja ‘twenty and one’ is tens first, like 二十一.
Luganda numerals follow the noun and agree with its class (abantu babiri ‘two people’, ebitabo bibiri ‘two books’); Chinese numerals come first and never agree: 两个人, 两本书.
Vietnamese numbers are built the same way (hai mươi mốt ‘two-ten-one’ ~ 二十一) and also need a classifier (hai quyển sách ~ 两本书).

Inuktitut’s traditional numbers are not decimal, and larger numbers are often borrowed today; the noun itself shows singular, dual or plural (inuk, inuuk, inuit). Chinese builds every number from ten digits and never marks number on the noun: 两个人.

seeAlso.note: German puts the units first (einundzwanzig, ‘one-and-twenty’) and has a plural after numbers (drei Bücher); Chinese says 二十一 in written order and the noun never changes.
Arabic numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender of the noun and decide its case and number; Chinese numbers never change — the measure word does the classifying.
Hebrew has a masculine and a feminine set of numbers chosen by the noun’s gender; Chinese has one set, and a measure word between number and noun.
